title: Robust Personalized Recommendation under Hidden Confounding in MNAR

paper.title: Robust Personalized Recommendation under Hidden Confounding in MNAR Thanks: † These authors contributed equally to this work. * Corresponding Author
paper.abstract: Abstract Recommender systems often rely on observational user–item interaction data, which is prone to selection bias due to users’ selective interactions with items. Inverse propensity weighting and doubly robust estimators effectively mitigate selection bias under observed confounding, but are unreliable in the presence of hidden confounders. Existing approaches relying on randomized controlled trials (RCTs) or global sensitivity bounds are constrained in practice: RCTs demand costly experimental data, while global sensitivity bounds presume a uniformly bounded effect of unmeasured confounders on propensities through sensitivity analysis, thereby neglecting heterogeneity across user–item interactions. To overcome this limitation, we propose a novel framework, which estimates user–item level sensitivity bounds, thereby substantially relaxing the homogeneity assumption inherent in global sensitivity bounds named Personalized Unobserved-Confounding-aware Interaction Deconfounder (PUID). To ensure both robustness and predictive accuracy, we further develop an adversarial optimization strategy and propose a benchmark-guided variant (BPUID) that incorporates pre-trained models as stabilizing references. Extensive experiments on three real-world datasets demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms global methods under hidden confounding, without requiring RCT data.

sections.heading: I Introduction
sections.text: Recommender systems are widely used to deliver personalized content across e‑commerce, social media, and lifestyle services [ 1 ] . Users typically interact with only a small portion of available items, preferring items they already like. As a result, interactions with less-preferred items are rarely observed. In recommender systems, missing data often follows a Missing Not At Random (MNAR) pattern, as user rating propensity depends on unobserved preferences [ 2 ] . This leads to bias when averaging observed ratings, since users more often rate liked items [ 3 , 4 ] . Similarly, ad‑placement systems favor popular items due to selection bias [ 5 ] . Modeling MNAR mechanisms helps improve recommendation quality and reduce bias [ 6 ] . To address selection bias, standard methods include error imputation [ 7 , 8 , 9 ] , inverse propensity weighting (IPW) [ 10 , 11 , 12 , 13 ] , and doubly robust estimation [ 14 , 12 , 15 ] . These methods assume all confounders are observed. However, unobserved confounders such as user intent, income, or demographics jointly affect exposure and feedback, making these methods ineffective. This hidden confounding poses a major challenge for unbiased recommendation evaluation [ 16 , 17 , 18 , 19 ] . Existing solutions to hidden confounding fall into two classes. Sensitivity‑analysis methods bound the influence of hidden confounders by restricting propensity scores to a plausible range via worst‑case optimization [ 16 , 20 ] . A leading approach, the Robust Deconfounder (RD), embeds such bounds into adversarial training to maintain stability under confounding [ 21 , 22 ] . Data‑fusion methods use auxiliary data from randomized controlled trials (RCTs) or A/B tests to calibrate propensity scores and imputation models [ 18 , 23 , 24 ] . Some balancing techniques incorporate unbiased RCT ratings to correct for unobserved confounders [ 18 ] . However, these approaches often require costly or ethically sensitive data collection [ 25 , 26 ] . Recent advances in sequential recommendation and large‑language‑model integration show promise for robustness under MNAR, yet challenges remain in handling correlated latent variables and adaptive causal structure [ 27 , 28 , 29 , 30 ] . To address these challenges, we propose a novel framework called Personalized Unobserved-Confounding-aware Interaction Deconfounder (PUID), which quantifies hidden confounding strength via user-item-specific sensitivity bounds. PUID employs a sensitivity analysis model to estimate personalized bounds on nominal propensity scores using observational data. To infer confounding strength, we introduce an entropy-based assumption that measures the contribution of unobserved confounders to reductions in observable entropy. Furthermore, we extend the model to a Benchmark-guided PUID (BPUID) that integrates a pre-trained model as a stabilizing reference, alleviating the trade-off between robustness and accuracy typical in worst-case optimization. The main contributions of this paper are summarized as follows: • To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to model personalized hidden confounding strength via user-item-specific bounds, enabling personalized estimation of confounding strength. • We develop an entropy-based sensitivity estimator using discretized information gain to infer confounding from observational data, and design an adversarial training strategy with a benchmark-guided extension (BPUID) to improve both robustness and prediction accuracy. • We conduct extensive experiments on three real-world datasets, demonstrating that the personalized approach significantly outperforms global methods and validates its effectiveness.

sections.heading: II Methodology
sections.text: We propose the Personalized Unobserved-confounding-aware Interaction Deconfounder (PUID), a method that addresses hidden confounding in recommender systems by estimating user–item-specific sensitivity bounds via entropy-based constraints while enhancing feature representation through matrix factorization.

sections.heading: II-A Problem Formulation
sections.text: Let 𝒰 \mathcal{U} and ℐ \mathcal{I} denote the complete sets of users and items, respectively. We consider 𝒰 o = { u 1 , … , u m } ⊆ 𝒰 \mathcal{U}_{o}=\{u_{1},\ldots,u_{m}\}\subseteq\mathcal{U} and ℐ o = { i 1 , … , i n } ⊆ ℐ \mathcal{I}_{o}=\{i_{1},\ldots,i_{n}\}\subseteq\mathcal{I} as the observed subsets of users and items, which are drawn randomly from the superpopulation. The user-item interaction space is defined as 𝒟 = 𝒰 o × ℐ o = { ( u , i ) ∣ u ∈ 𝒰 o , i ∈ ℐ o } \mathcal{D}=\mathcal{U}_{o}\times\mathcal{I}_{o}=\{(u,i)\mid u\in\mathcal{U}_{o},i\in\mathcal{I}_{o}\} . For each user-item pair ( u , i ) ∈ 𝒟 (u,i)\in\mathcal{D} , let x u , i ∈ ℝ K x_{u,i}\in\mathbb{R}^{K} denote the associated feature vector, r u , i ∈ ℝ r_{u,i}\in\mathbb{R} the true rating, and o u , i ∈ { 0 , 1 } o_{u,i}\in\{0,1\} a binary indicator that specifies whether r u , i r_{u,i} is observed. The set of all observed interactions is defined as 𝒪 = { ( u , i ) ∈ 𝒟 ∣ o u , i = 1 } . \mathcal{O}=\{(u,i)\in\mathcal{D}\mid o_{u,i}=1\}. In practice, the true rating r u , i r_{u,i} is only partially observed, rendering the prediction error e u , i e_{u,i} inaccessible when o u , i = 0 o_{u,i}=0 . A common approach is to minimize the naive loss ℒ Naive ​ ( ϕ ) = | 𝒪 | − 1 ​ ∑ ( u , i ) ∈ 𝒪 e u , i \mathcal{L}_{\text{Naive}}(\phi)=|\mathcal{O}|^{-1}\sum_{(u,i)\in\mathcal{O}}e_{u,i} , which relies solely on the observed interactions. Conventional estimators suffer from selection bias, deviating from the ideal loss and yielding biased estimates [ 15 ] . To address this, many methods reweight observed samples adopting propensity scores p u , i p_{u,i} , resulting in the Inverse Propensity Scoring (IPS) loss ℒ IPS ​ ( ϕ ) = | 𝒟 | − 1 ​ ∑ ( u , i ) ∈ 𝒟 o u , i ⋅ e u , i / p ^ u , i \mathcal{L}_{\text{IPS}}(\phi)=|\mathcal{D}|^{-1}\sum_{(u,i)\in\mathcal{D}}o_{u,i}\cdot e_{u,i}/\hat{p}_{u,i} , where p ^ u , i = π ⁡ ( x u , i , θ p ) \hat{p}_{u,i}=\pi(x_{u,i};\theta_{p}) denotes the estimated propensity score. The IPS estimator remains unbiased provided that p ^ u , i \hat{p}_{u,i} exactly matches the true propensity p ^ u , i \hat{p}_{u,i} [ 13 , 15 ] . The Doubly Robust (DR) estimator addresses the high variance of IPS by combining propensity weighting with error imputation, thereby improving robustness [ 15 , 31 , 18 ] . Its formulation is: ℒ DR ​ ( ϕ , θ ) = 1 | 𝒟 | ​ ∑ ( u , i ) ∈ 𝒟 [ e ^ u , i + o u , i ⋅ ( e u , i − e ^ u , i ) p ^ u , i ] , \mathcal{L}_{\text{DR}}(\phi,\theta)=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}|}\sum_{(u,i)\in\mathcal{D}}\left[\hat{e}_{u,i}+\frac{o_{u,i}\cdot(e_{u,i}-\hat{e}_{u,i})}{\hat{p}_{u,i}}\right], (1) where e ^ u , i = m ⁡ ( x u , i , θ e ) \hat{e}_{u,i}=m(x_{u,i};\theta_{e}) denotes the imputed error from an auxiliary model. The DR estimator remains unbiased if either the estimated propensity scores or imputed errors are accurate.

sections.text: In exposure modeling, unobserved confounders can reduce outcome uncertainty o u , i o_{u,i} similarly to observed factors. We formalize this via entropy-ratio constraints for residual information gain: H ⁡ ( o u , i ) − H ⁡ ( o u , i ∣ x u ) H ⁡ ( o u , i ∣ x u , x i ) − H ⁡ ( o u , i ∣ x u , x i , h u ) > 0 , \frac{H(o_{u,i})-H(o_{u,i}\mid x_{u})}{H(o_{u,i}\mid x_{u},x_{i})-H(o_{u,i}\mid x_{u},x_{i},h_{u})}>0, (2) H ⁡ ( o u , i ∣ x u ) − H ⁡ ( o u , i ∣ x u , x i ) H ⁡ ( o u , i ∣ x u , x i , h u ) − H ⁡ ( o u , i ∣ x u , x i , h u , h i ) > 0 . \frac{H(o_{u,i}\mid x_{u})-H(o_{u,i}\mid x_{u},x_{i})}{H(o_{u,i}\mid x_{u},x_{i},h_{u})-H(o_{u,i}\mid x_{u},x_{i},h_{u},h_{i})}>0. (3) Here, H H is entropy, x u , x i x_{u},x_{i} are observed features, and h u , h i h_{u},h_{i} are unobserved confounders. These ratios encode that hidden confounders reduce entropy analogously to observed factors, capturing residual exposure informativeness. From an information-theoretic perspective, h u , i h_{u,i} maintains positive conditional mutual information with the outcome given observed features, i.e., I ⁡ ( o ; h | x ) = H ⁡ ( o | x ) − H ⁡ ( o | x , h ) > 0 I(o;h|x)=H(o|x)-H(o|x,h)>0 . This ensures that both observed features (numerators) and hidden confounders (denominators) contribute positive reductions in entropy, consistent with latent‑variable causal discovery in high‑dimensional settings [ 32 ] . To operationalize this, we define a surrogate hidden-confounding impact metric: IG h ∝ α ⋅ [ H ⁡ ( o u , i ) − H ⁡ ( o u , i ∣ x u ) ] + β ⋅ [ H ( o u , i ∣ x u ) − H ( o u , i ∣ x u , x i ) ] , \begin{split}\mathrm{IG}_{h}\propto\ &\alpha\cdot\left[H(o_{u,i})-H(o_{u,i}\mid x_{u})\right]\\ &+\beta\cdot\left[H(o_{u,i}\mid x_{u})-H(o_{u,i}\mid x_{u},x_{i})\right],\end{split} (4) The proportionality symbol indicates that only relative magnitude matters, not absolute scale. Hence, IG h \mathrm{IG}_{h} acts as a causal proxy for unobserved confounding strength, being proportional to I ⁡ ( o ; h | x ) I(o;h|x) , and quantifies residual exposure informativeness beyond observed variables. This personalized approach avoids the over-conservatism or over-optimism of uniform constraints and enables finer-grained bias control. It also retains a well-defined uncertainty set over propensity scores, thereby facilitating rigorous adversarial optimization for robust estimation.

sections.heading: III Experiments
sections.text: We conduct experiments to answer following research questions: • RQ1 : Do the proposed PUID and BPUID methods outperform existing methods under conditions of hidden confounding? • RQ2 : Do our methods stably perform well under scenarios with different levels of hidden confounding?

sections.heading: III-A Experimental Settings
sections.text: Dataset and Preprocessing. We evaluate PUID and BPUID on three public datasets: KuaiRec , Coat , and Yahoo!R3 . Each contains both biased and unbiased interactions. KuaiRec has 1.3M biased and 0.27M unbiased interactions from 7,176 users and 10,729 items; Coat includes 6,960/4,640 interactions; Yahoo!R3 has 311,704/54,000 interactions. For KuaiRec, we perform correlation-based feature selection and discretization, retaining 19 item and 14 user features. For ID-only datasets (Coat and Yahoo!R3), we generate pseudo-features using matrix factorization and clustering. To simulate exposure bias, we downsample unbiased interactions based on estimated propensities and create masked subsets with 10–80% removal to test robustness under sparsity. Compared Methods. We compare the proposed PUID and BPUID against several representative baselines, all built upon a unified feature-aware matrix factorization (MF-MLPs) backbone that fuses IDs and side features via MLPs. The compared methods include: • Base : Standard MF-MLPs trained on biased data [ 33 ] . • RCT-free methods : IPS [ 13 ] , DR [ 15 ] ; RD [ 16 ] , BRD-IPS/BRD-DR [ 16 ] ; Multi-IPS/Multi-DR [ 34 ] . • PUID-IPS/PUID-DR : Our methods enhancing IPS/DR with personalized sensitivity bounds. • BPUID-IPS/BPUID-DR : Variants adding benchmark-guided regularization for improved stability. Evaluation Metrics. We evaluate model performance using UAUC and NDCG@K . For COAT and Yahoo!R3 datasets, we use NDCG@5; for KuaiRec, we use NDCG@50.

sections.heading: III-B Performance Comparison (RQ1)
sections.text: As shown in Table I , PUID and BPUID consistently outperform baselines across all datasets. PUID‑IPS uses personalized bounds to reweight each user–item pair, achieving stable gains under varying sparsity. PUID‑DR attains the highest accuracy among doubly‑robust estimators through personalized bounds and error imputation, effectively mitigating propensity bias. BPUID variants further improve robustness in sparse or noisy settings via benchmark‑guided regularization, delivering substantial gains on Coat and Yahoo!R3. While PUID excels with sufficient data, BPUID handles sparsity more effectively. sections.heading: IV Conclusion and future work
sections.text: This work addresses hidden confounding in debiased recommendation, a critical challenge that limits the reliability of conventional propensity-based methods (e.g., IPS, DR) and global sensitivity bound approaches. Conventional methods either rely on unrealistic assumptions of observed confounders or neglect heterogeneity across user–item interactions, while RCT-based solutions suffer from costly data collection. To overcome these limitations, we propose PUID, a novel framework that infers user-item-specific sensitivity bounds via entropy-based information gain, enabling personalized confounding adjustment. We further extend PUID to BPUID by integrating benchmark-guided regularization, alleviating the trade-off between robustness and predictive accuracy inherent in worst-case optimization. Extensive experiments on three real-world datasets demonstrate that both PUID and BPUID significantly outperform global methods under hidden confounding, validating the effectiveness of personalized robust optimization without requiring RCT data. Our proposed framework, while advancing personalized debiasing under hidden confounding, its efficacy may still affected by some potential issues. The estimation of entropy-based sensitivity may be influenced by the chosen discretization strategy, while the robustness of personalized bounds relies on score range normalization and interval calibration. Furthermore, the framework’s generalizability is connected to the capacity of the underlying representation model, and hyperparameter selection inherently balances the trade off between user and item side impacts. Future work will explore more flexible discretization approaches, optimized calibration protocols, integration with advanced representation learning paradigms, and systematic hyperparameter sensitivity analysis to enhance the framework’s adaptability and robustness to diverse data scenarios.

Inverse propensity weighting and doubly robust estimators effectively mitigate selection bias under observed confounding, but are unreliable in the presence of hidden confounders. Existing approaches relying on randomized controlled trials (RCTs) or global sensitivity bounds are constrained in practice: RCTs demand costly experimental data, while global sensitivity bounds presume a uniformly bounded effect of unmeasured confounders on propensities through sensitivity analysis, thereby neglecting heterogeneity across user–item interactions. To overcome this limitation, we propose a novel framework, which estimates user–item level sensitivity bounds, thereby substantially relaxing the homogeneity assumption inherent in global sensitivity bounds named Personalized Unobserved-Confounding-aware Interaction Deconfounder (PUID). To ensure both robustness and predictive accuracy, we further develop an adversarial optimization strategy and propose a benchmark-guided variant (BPUID) that incorporates pre-trained models as stabilizing references. Extensive experiments on three real-world datasets demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms global methods under hidden confounding, without requiring RCT data. Index Terms: Recommendation Systems, Selection bias, Hidden confounding, Sensitivity analysis I Introduction Recommender systems are widely used to deliver personalized content across e‑commerce, social media, and lifestyle services [ 1 ] . Users typically interact with only a small portion of available items, preferring items they already like. As a result, interactions with less-preferred items are rarely observed. In recommender systems, missing data often follows a Missing Not At Random (MNAR) pattern, as user rating propensity depends on unobserved preferences [ 2 ] . This leads to bias when averaging observed ratings, since users more often rate liked items [ 3 , 4 ] . Similarly, ad‑placement systems favor popular items due to selection bias [ 5 ] . Modeling MNAR mechanisms helps improve recommendation quality and reduce bias [ 6 ] . To address selection bias, standard methods include error imputation [ 7 , 8 , 9 ] , inverse propensity weighting (IPW) [ 10 , 11 , 12 , 13 ] , and doubly robust estimation [ 14 , 12 , 15 ] . These methods assume all confounders are observed. However, unobserved confounders such as user intent, income, or demographics jointly affect exposure and feedback, making these methods ineffective. This hidden confounding poses a major challenge for unbiased recommendation evaluation [ 16 , 17 , 18 , 19 ] . Existing solutions to hidden confounding fall into two classes. Sensitivity‑analysis methods bound the influence of hidden confounders by restricting propensity scores to a plausible range via worst‑case optimization [ 16 , 20 ] . A leading approach, the Robust Deconfounder (RD), embeds such bounds into adversarial training to maintain stability under confounding [ 21 , 22 ] . Data‑fusion methods use auxiliary data from randomized controlled trials (RCTs) or A/B tests to calibrate propensity scores and imputation models [ 18 , 23 , 24 ] . Some balancing techniques incorporate unbiased RCT ratings to correct for unobserved confounders [ 18 ] . However, these approaches often require costly or ethically sensitive data collection [ 25 , 26 ] . Recent advances in sequential recommendation and large‑language‑model integration show promise for robustness under MNAR, yet challenges remain in handling correlated latent variables and adaptive causal structure [ 27 , 28 , 29 , 30 ] . To address these challenges, we propose a novel framework called Personalized Unobserved-Confounding-aware Interaction Deconfounder (PUID), which quantifies hidden confounding strength via user-item-specific sensitivity bounds. PUID employs a sensitivity analysis model to estimate personalized bounds on nominal propensity scores using observational data. To infer confounding strength, we introduce an entropy-based assumption that measures the contribution of unobserved confounders to reductions in observable entropy. Furthermore, we extend the model to a Benchmark-guided PUID (BPUID) that integrates a pre-trained model as a stabilizing reference, alleviating the trade-off between robustness and accuracy typical in worst-case optimization. The main contributions of this paper are summarized as follows: • To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to model personalized hidden confounding strength via user-item-specific bounds, enabling personalized estimation of confounding strength. • We develop an entropy-based sensitivity estimator using discretized information gain to infer confounding from observational data, and design an adversarial training strategy with a benchmark-guided extension (BPUID) to improve both robustness and prediction accuracy. • We conduct extensive experiments on three real-world datasets, demonstrating that the personalized approach significantly outperforms global methods and validates its effectiveness. II Methodology We propose the Personalized Unobserved-confounding-aware Interaction Deconfounder (PUID), a method that addresses hidden confounding in recommender systems by estimating user–item-specific sensitivity bounds via entropy-based constraints while enhancing feature representation through matrix factorization. II-A Problem Formulation Let 𝒰 \mathcal{U} and ℐ \mathcal{I} denote the complete sets of users and items, respectively. III Experiments We conduct experiments to answer following research questions: • RQ1 : Do the proposed PUID and BPUID methods outperform existing methods under conditions of hidden confounding? • RQ2 : Do our methods stably perform well under scenarios with different levels of hidden confounding? III-A Experimental Settings Dataset and Preprocessing. We evaluate PUID and BPUID on three public datasets: KuaiRec , Coat , and Yahoo!R3 . Each contains both biased and unbiased interactions. KuaiRec has 1.3M biased and 0.27M unbiased interactions from 7,176 users and 10,729 items; Coat includes 6,960/4,640 interactions; Yahoo!R3 has 311,704/54,000 interactions. For KuaiRec, we perform correlation-based feature selection and discretization, retaining 19 item and 14 user features. For ID-only datasets (Coat and Yahoo!R3), we generate pseudo-features using matrix factorization and clustering. To simulate exposure bias, we downsample unbiased interactions based on estimated propensities and create masked subsets with 10–80% removal to test robustness under sparsity. Compared Methods. We compare the proposed PUID and BPUID against several representative baselines, all built upon a unified feature-aware matrix factorization (MF-MLPs) backbone that fuses IDs and side features via MLPs. The compared methods include: • Base : Standard MF-MLPs trained on biased data [ 33 ] . • RCT-free methods : IPS [ 13 ] , DR [ 15 ] ; RD [ 16 ] , BRD-IPS/BRD-DR [ 16 ] ; Multi-IPS/Multi-DR [ 34 ] . • PUID-IPS/PUID-DR : Our methods enhancing IPS/DR with personalized sensitivity bounds. • BPUID-IPS/BPUID-DR : Variants adding benchmark-guided regularization for improved stability. Evaluation Metrics. We evaluate model performance using UAUC and NDCG@K . For COAT and Yahoo!R3 datasets, we use NDCG@5; for KuaiRec, we use NDCG@50. III-B Performance Comparison (RQ1) As shown in Table I , PUID and BPUID consistently outperform baselines across all datasets. PUID‑IPS uses personalized bounds to reweight each user–item pair, achieving stable gains under varying sparsity. PUID‑DR attains the highest accuracy among doubly‑robust estimators through personalized bounds and error imputation, effectively mitigating propensity bias. BPUID variants further improve robustness in sparse or noisy settings via benchmark‑guided regularization, delivering substantial gains on Coat and Yahoo!R3. While PUID excels with sufficient data, BPUID handles sparsity more effectively. Both significantly surpass global‑bound and shared‑representation methods, confirming that personalized robust optimization successfully alleviates hidden confounding. Conventional methods either rely on unrealistic assumptions of observed confounders or neglect heterogeneity across user–item interactions, while RCT-based solutions suffer from costly data collection. To overcome these limitations, we propose PUID, a novel framework that infers user-item-specific sensitivity bounds via entropy-based information gain, enabling personalized confounding adjustment. We further extend PUID to BPUID by integrating benchmark-guided regularization, alleviating the trade-off between robustness and predictive accuracy inherent in worst-case optimization. Extensive experiments on three real-world datasets demonstrate that both PUID and BPUID significantly outperform global methods under hidden confounding, validating the effectiveness of personalized robust optimization without requiring RCT data. Our proposed framework, while advancing personalized debiasing under hidden confounding, its efficacy may still affected by some potential issues. The estimation of entropy-based sensitivity may be influenced by the chosen discretization strategy, while the robustness of personalized bounds relies on score range normalization and interval calibration. Furthermore, the framework’s generalizability is connected to the capacity of the underlying representation model, and hyperparameter selection inherently balances the trade off between user and item side impacts. Future work will explore more flexible discretization approaches, optimized calibration protocols, integration with advanced representation learning paradigms, and systematic hyperparameter sensitivity analysis to enhance the framework’s adaptability and robustness to diverse data scenarios.
